title: kv-cache-prefetch-eviction-pcie-fallback-draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a working design for a multi-tier KV cache policy that favors prefetching frequently re-used KV blocks back into GPU memory while gracefully offloading low-value blocks to host memory over PCIe or to UMA paths. Goal is to minimize tail latency regressions during bursty traffic and reduce per-token cost by avoiding unnecessary full model loads or recomputations.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to transformer KV caches used by the streaming/generation path in the runtime.
- Target SLOs: median token latency within baseline +/-5%, P99 within +15% under heavy load.
- Hardware: heterogeneous fleet — discrete GPUs with PCIe (Gen3/4), and a subset of machines with integrated GPU+CPU (UMA). Some hosts include NVMe local swap for emergency eviction.
- Assumes runtime supports async DMA, pinned host buffers, and compress/decompress kernels (int8/4/2 quantization) on-GPU.

Design principles:
1) Tiered storage with escalating cost:
   - Tier 0: GPU DRAM (full precision or quantized in GPU memory) — fastest.
   - Tier 1: GPU compressed slab (lower precision or packed cache) — still GPU-resident but smaller per-key.
   - Tier 2: Host DRAM over PCIe (pinned pinned buffers, async DMA) — moderate latency; capacity large.
   - Tier 3: UMA path (CPU-accessible GPU memory) — variable latency depending on platform; prefer when PCIe bandwidth saturated or on UMA hosts.
   - Tier 4: NVMe/Persistent swap (last resort) — high latency, used only for long-lived but infrequent keys.

2) Evict-by-value, not purely recency: each KV block scored by a composite utility function that accounts for recency, frequency, last-requested-step-distance (estimated time until next reuse), and cost to retrieve (PCIe vs UMA vs decompression cost).

Scoring function (conceptual):
   score(k) = w_r * recency_score(k) + w_f * frequency_score(k) + w_p * predicted_reuse(k) - w_c * retrieval_cost(k)
   - recency_score: exponentially decayed counter (last access time).
   - frequency_score: sliding window hit count normalized by key size.
   - predicted_reuse: model-driven predictor (see below) returning probability in [0,1] that key will be reused in next N tokens.
   - retrieval_cost: estimated latency to bring key back to Tier 0 (measured online).

Weights are tunable; suggested starting point: w_r=0.5, w_f=0.3, w_p=0.15, w_c=0.05. These bias toward keeping recently-used items while allowing frequency & reuse prediction to rescue hot-but-not-recent keys.

Prefetch policy:
- When a request causes a KV block to be promoted from Tier 2/3 to Tier 0 because serving it from host would violate latency SLO for the request, the runtime will opportunistically prefetch adjacent KV blocks that have high predicted_reuse and low retrieval_cost.
- Prefetch budget: a soft limit of X bytes per second per GPU (configurable); default 64MB/s. Prefetches are deprioritized when observed P95 latency exceeds threshold or when GPU kernel queue depth is high.
- Prefetch granularity: group by attention-head blobs or continuous key spans of tokens (aligned to KV allocation).

Offload modes and thresholds:
- Two operating modes: conservative and aggressive. Conservative favors latency (less offload), aggressive favors capacity/utilization (more offload).
- Default thresholds (conservative):
   - GPU occupancy percent = total_KV_usage / gpu_kv_capacity.
   - If occupancy > 70% start evicting to Tier 1 (GPU compressed).
   - If occupancy > 85% begin offloading low-score blocks to Tier 2 (PCIe host).
   - If PCIe queue depth > 75% or observed DMA latency > baseline*1.4 then slow down offload and favor UMA path if available.
- Aggressive mode lowers thresholds by ~10 percentage points and increases allowed prefetch bandwidth.

UMA handling specifics:
- On UMA-capable hosts, retrieval_cost for UMA = measured UMA memcpy latency which can be lower than PCIe for small block sizes but may be higher for large contiguous transfers.
- UMA preference heuristic: prefer UMA if current PCIe utilization > 60% and UMA measured latency < PCIe_latency * 1.1.
- UMA fallback path must be tested per host during boot (microbenchmarks) to populate per-host latency models. These are cached in host profile config.

Kernel and scheduling implications:
- IO threads and GPU compute threads must coordinate through a prioritized work queue. KV retrievals that are on the critical path for an in-flight token must be classified 'urgent' and scheduled before background prefetches.
- Background compaction and compression tasks run at low priority; if kernel queue depth for generation kernels rises above threshold, background tasks yield.
- DMA submission should use batched descriptors to the NIC/driver when multiple blocks target the same host page to reduce PCIe overhead.
- Provide per-request QoS token: requests flagged with strict latency_slo will pin required KV blocks in Tier 0 for the duration of processing (if available); do not evict until response complete. Pinning is limited by a global pin budget (e.g., 5% of GPU KV capacity) to avoid starvation.

I/O scheduler and fairness:
- Implement a hybrid priority scheduler: urgent retrievals (on-path) -> reprioritized prefetches -> compaction -> low-priority background offload.
- Fairness across concurrent requests: weight retrieval scheduling by request priority and a time-since-last-served metric so long-lived sessions cannot monopolize PCIe bandwidth.

Compression and format ladder:
- Before offloading to host, attempt in-GPU compression to Tier 1 format (e.g., 4-bit quantized KV) when compute budget is available and compression is net-positive (test shows >20% space savings with <2ms latency impact for blocks >8KB).
- If compressed GPU slabs still exceed capacity, prefer moving full blocks to host rather than repeatedly compress/decompress small hot blocks.

Observability and telemetry:
- Emit the following per-GPU metrics: KV_tier_bytes[tier=0..4], eviction_count[tier_from][tier_to], average_retrieval_latency_ms[tier], pci_e_util_pct, uma_util_metric, prefetch_bytes_per_min, prefetch_hit_rate, pinned_bytes, pinned_requests_count.
- Log examples when retrieval_cost estimates diverge from actual by >50% for online tuning.

Adaptive learning and tuning:
- Maintain lightweight online learner for predicted_reuse using per-model small LSTM or exponentially-weighted Markov predictor (simple n-gram on token offsets is acceptable initial implementation). Predictor input: sequence position, session id, past reuse patterns. Output: probability for next-N reuse.
- Periodically recalibrate retrieval_cost using microbenchmarks (background) to account for PCIe contention and host noise.

Safety nets and degradation modes:
- If P99 token latency exceeds SLO by >2x, temporarily suspend prefetches and aggressive offloads, and preferentially promote Tier 2 objects back to Tier 0 if already in-flight or requested recently.
- If DMA errors or PCIe driver faults observed, mark host as degraded and fall back to UMA or block new offloads.

Rollout plan and experiments:
1) Canary (week 0–2): enable scoring + Tier 1 compression only on 5% of serving fleet for a single model with stable traffic. Collect metrics: prefetch hit, eviction rate, P50/P95/P99 token latency, cost per token.
2) A/B (week 3–5): enable Tier 2 (PCIe) offload on 20% of traffic for medium-size models; compare end-to-end latency and GPU utilization.
3) Broad enable (week 6+): add UMA heuristics and predictor adjustments, enable dynamic thresholds, monitor regressions.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to efficiently represent and batch small KV blocks for PCIe to avoid high per-transfer overhead? (Kernel-level aggregation vs runtime coalescing)
- Exact weight tuning for scoring function — initial values provided, need offline sims + online tuning.
- How aggressive should pinning be for RLHF-style long sessions? Investigate session-level policies.
- NVMe swap protocol and safety limits (we need eviction QoS to avoid saturating host I/O).

Next steps (action items):
- Spike: implement microbenchmark harness to measure per-host PCIe/UMA retrieval cost (owner: Ethan Li) — 2 weeks.
- Spike: simple n-gram reuse predictor and simulator to evaluate scoring weights on recorded traces (owner: Maya Gupta) — 3 weeks.
- Prototype: Tier 1 compression path and async prefetch queue with backpressure signals (owner: Riley Chen) — 4 weeks.
- Design review: schedule with infra, sre, and kernel teams to discuss driver-level batching & pinned buffer management (owner: Riley Chen) — next week.

Appendix: quick heuristics cheatsheet (defaults)
- Start compressing at GPU occupancy > 70%.
- Start offloading to host at occupancy > 85%.
- Prefetch bandwidth: 64MB/s default, cap prefetch when P95 latency > baseline*1.2.
- PCIe saturation threshold: 75% queue depth.
- Pin budget: 5% of GPU KV capacity.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic; focuses first on keeping tail latency intact while reclaiming capacity. Expect multiple iterations — the scoring system should be implemented in a configurable way so ops can tune weights without code changes.
- Please annotate linked artifacts (PR/JIRA) with any relevant experiments or historical data you have.
